title: Business Person at Lunch — Awareness → Newsletter Subscription
subtitle: How a weekday professional and an office/catering coordinator turn a reliable brisket lunch into load-bearing routine — and opt in for operational signal.

stages.name: Group & Catering
stages.sub: brings the team / orders for the office

doing.text: A colleague points at the truck on the walk back from a meeting — "the brisket one" is the whole pitch. The catering coordinator arrives differently: a team offsite surfaces it, then she immediately checks whether they cater, can invoice, and will actually show up.

thinking.text: "Is this fast enough for a workday, and can I trust it?" The solo professional screens for time cost; the coordinator screens for whether it can carry a group booking she'd stake her name on.

channels.text: A trusted colleague's word of mouth and sheer proximity to the office; for the coordinator, an offsite recommendation and the borderblend.ca website she goes hunting on for a "book us" option.

pains.text: There's no obvious front door for the group buyer — the catering path is buried behind a site built for the person buying one taco, so a high-intent lead has to dig to learn if BorderBlend even serves her use case.

opps.text: Capture the referral moment and make the group/catering path discoverable from first contact — a clear "cater your team" route alongside the consumer menu, so the coordinator who is already looking can find the door immediately.

doing.text: The professional stands in the 12:40 line once — reluctantly — and orders the smoked brisket taco. The coordinator vets it on her own lunch before she'll ever put her name on a team order: "I will never put my name on something I haven't eaten myself."

thinking.text: "Very good brisket in six minutes — eighty percent of the restaurant for twenty percent of the time cost." The food registers even in work mode; the coordinator confirms it clears the bar of "not sad-tray-of-sandwiches good."

channels.text: The truck window and the in-person board — the first-hand product experience, not the app or social. The lunch line is the whole channel.

pains.text: A line at 12:40 is a real risk to a 1 o'clock meeting, and the hero can vanish — brisket sold out by early Saturday afternoon on the coordinator's first solo visit. Execution variability threatens the very first impression.

opps.text: Let the product do the converting it already does — protect that first taste with reliable stock and a predictable line, and lean on the plant-based over-delivery that surprises even sceptics, so trial reliably becomes rotation.

doing.text: It quietly enters the rotation — "I didn't decide to become a regular. It happened" — two-to-four lunches a week. The coordinator moves BorderBlend onto her shortlist of trusted vendors for Friday treats and monthly team lunches.

thinking.text: "I don't need the best brisket in the city — I need very good brisket in six minutes." Lunch is now a solved problem he refuses to re-solve daily; reliability and sameness beat novelty.

channels.text: Walk-up to the known truck, working off a remembered schedule; a first curious tap on the app to try ordering ahead.

pains.text: The one question every workday — is this specific truck open right now, and where — often has no reliable answer until he's standing on an empty corner. Price creep ("almost the same as a restaurant now") begins to register in the background.

opps.text: Answering "open now, where, how long's the line" reliably — plus working order-ahead — converts an already-earned habit into daily use. Fixing app/POS sync turns the highest-intent repeat customer into load-bearing routine.

doing.text: The professional becomes the "I'll grab lunch — what does everyone want" person two-to-four times a week, taking three or four orders in one trip. The coordinator books team lunches and client catering for ~30, sends out a dietary form, and plans over email and a phone call with the local operator.

thinking.text: "If I could pre-load a group order, that's me bringing them four customers instead of one." For the coordinator: "Reliability is the whole game — will you actually show up, at the headcount I said." The food is table stakes; trust is the decision.

channels.text: A buried catering page on borderblend.ca, a booking form, back-and-forth email and one phone call; a crumpled thermal receipt or nothing where an invoice should be.

pains.text: Ingredient-level allergen info is genuinely hard to get — with a tree-nut/EpiPen colleague at stake, no straight answer means she doesn't book at all. Confirmations are casual ("yep we'll be there!") when she needs a hard, forwardable booking for her VP; invoicing is informal; there's no clear front door for the professional "waving money" for catering.

opps.text: Ring-fence and reserve stock for booked group orders (never first-come), issue a hard forwardable confirmation, attach an ingredient-level allergen sheet, and provide a proper itemised invoice (GST broken out, PO reference) plus a clear catering price sheet and booking door — every one earns the loyalty of a buyer purchasing for 30, monthly, year-round.

doing.text: The professional now runs part of his workday around the truck — and downloads the app specifically to order ahead, uses it twice, then closes it. The coordinator carries the whole relationship: she has to remember they exist, dig up the booking form each time, and solve the Calgary winter herself.

thinking.text: "It stops being the truck I take my chances on and becomes infrastructure — you don't churn out of infrastructure." For the coordinator: "It's all on me to initiate," and a food truck in a minus-25 February is a hard sell that needs an indoor answer.

channels.text: The app and its order-ahead flow — where the menu didn't match the truck board, he couldn't tell if the truck was open, and there was no clear "your order is ready" moment; a POS that doesn't sync; a seasonal calendar with a winter hole.

pains.text: App↔POS sync failures and a static menu that doesn't match the board let the highest-intent users down; order-ahead shows 44% drop-off and pickup-location confirmation abandons at checkout. Meanwhile the coordinator has no winter/indoor catering path and shoulders every re-initiation herself.

opps.text: Reliable order-ahead with a genuine ready-for-pickup handoff turns a two-time app abandoner into daily infrastructure; a proactive seasonal prompt and a winter/indoor catering option means the coordinator no longer carries the initiation — the brand comes to her at the right moment.

doing.text: Both are habitual unsubscribers who opt in anyway — narrowly. The professional signs up for high-signal lunch alerts; the coordinator says "for the group side? A hundred percent yes," the strongest possible tell from someone who unsubscribes from everything.

thinking.text: "Signal versus noise." Brand story, meet-the-team, recipes = unsubscribe in four seconds. "Truck is here today," actionable specials, and a booking path = open every time. The coordinator: "Talk to me like I'm running an operation, because I am."

channels.text: An operational email newsletter, a morning "truck is here today" push, and a real catering booking system with a hard confirmation and a day-before reminder — not brand-story content.

pains.text: The existing loyalty programme is opaque enough that regulars don't know it exists or abandon the account interface (33% drop-off on loyalty search), and any generic push or brand-story email triggers an instant unsubscribe — so the current offer converts neither buyer.

opps.text: The converting offer is purely operational: "truck is here today" morning lunch alerts and reliable pre-order for the professional; a catering menu with allergen sheet forwardable in one shot, real availability, a hard "we're confirmed in writing" booking with a day-before reminder, and clean itemised invoicing for the coordinator — plus seasonal open/close prompts and a simple, visible loyalty scheme. Give them the boring, load-bearing stuff and they subscribe and book constantly.
